name: Opportunity Green (Giving Green, 2026)
summary: Law, policy and economics to cut emissions from aviation and shipping. A re-implementation of Giving Green's estimate of what Opportunity Green's work with climate-vulnerable countries at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), and its submission to the international law of the sea tribunal, cost per tonne of CO₂e avoided.

sections.title: From cost per tonne to tonnes per dollar
sections.explainer: charityevals' step after Giving Green's bottom line: Giving Green reports dollars per tonne; the site needs tonnes per dollar, and how much air pollution those tonnes cut. The tonnes come from ships burning cleaner fuel or less of it; ship smoke per tonne of CO₂ is about the world average, and only part of it goes with each well-to-wake tonne cut (docs/normalization.md 2.5). The tonnes come years after the money is spent, so they are discounted for that wait at the site's discount rate.

sections.title: Staff pay below market
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not Giving Green's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere counts as an in-kind contribution and gets its share of the outcome. Off by default.

rows.label: …is x times as cost-effective as the top recommendation benchmark
Years from the grant until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: Opportunity Green's spending is 2023–25; Giving Green's tonnes are the gap between high-ambition and business-as-usual shipping rules from 2025, which closes within 5 years in its best guess (10 in its high-impact case) as the business-as-usual rules catch up. So the tonnes come mostly in the late 2020s, about four years after the money, 2 to 8. Our judgment from Giving Green's dates. Giving Green counts a tonne the same whenever it is avoided; the site discounts every future benefit at the discount rate under Your values, in both views (an evaluator stating dollars per tonne takes no view on discounting). The heat deaths a tonne avoids are discounted again from the year it is avoided, in the site's climate conversion.

rows.label: How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: Your value, one figure for every model built on an organisation's past average (Your values: "How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far"): the cost per tonne is Opportunity Green's past IMO and ITLOS spending over its expected effect, an average; the next dollar does less than the average dollar did, since an organisation pursues its best opportunities first. 50% by default (our judgment), from 18% to 100% (average = marginal). The evaluator view keeps 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar
rows.explainer: One over Giving Green's cost per tonne, discounted for the wait until the tonnes are avoided, like every future benefit on the site. How much air pollution these tonnes cut is the rows below. A marginal dollar is counted at the share of the past average you set (row above).

rows.label: Share of ship smoke that goes with each tonne cut

source.title: Zhang et al. (2021), Mortality reduction relative to implementing new shipping emissions policy (scenario study), Environmental Research Letters 16, 084015 (MIT)
source.note: About 94,000 deaths in 2015 from shipping's fine particles; the 0.5% sulphur cap avoids about 30,000 a year; a Tier III NOx standard would avoid about 33,000 more.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, with a wide range. The IMO's standard lowers the greenhouse-gas intensity of ship fuel more than how much is burned. Fuel burned less (efficiency, slower steaming) cuts all its smoke with each tonne. Fuel switched to ammonia, methanol or biofuels cuts the sulphur and most of the particles but not the NOx, and after the 2020 sulphur cap NOx drives about half of ship smoke deaths (Zhang et al. 2021: a NOx standard would avoid about 33,000 of the remaining ~64,000). Part of each well-to-wake tonne is upstream fuel supply, far from people. Best guess half; low 0.2 (mostly fuel switching, much of it upstream); high 1 (liquefied gas removes sulphur, particles and most NOx while cutting only 15–20% of well-to-wake CO₂e, which puts a lot of smoke on each tonne).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of CO₂ from ships, relative to the fossil-fuel average

source.title: Sofiev et al. (2018), Cleaner fuels for ships provide public health benefits with climate tradeoffs, Nature Communications; Zhang et al. (2021), Environmental Research Letters
source.note: Sofiev: about 266,000 deaths a year from ship emissions after the 2020 sulphur limit. Zhang (https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ac146b): about 94,000 in 2015, less about 30,000 avoided by the sulphur limit. IMO, Fourth GHG Study 2020 (https://www.imo.org/en/ourwork/Environment/Pages/Fourth-IMO-Greenhouse-Gas-Study-2020.aspx): total shipping CO₂ 1,056 million tonnes in 2018.

rows.explainer: Ship smoke per tonne of CO₂ after the 2020 sulphur limit. Sofiev et al. (2018) estimate about 266,000 deaths a year from about 870 million tonnes of CO₂, 3.1 per 10,000 tonnes: 2.1 times the world average of 1.46. Zhang et al. (2021) find about 94,000 in 2015, of which the sulphur limit avoids about 30,000, leaving about 64,000 from 1,056 million tonnes of shipping CO₂ (IMO's Fourth GHG Study, 2018): 0.6 per 10,000, 0.42 of the average. The two studies span the range; the best guess, 0.94, is their middle on a log scale.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: The row the site's climate conversion reads (docs/normalization.md 2.5): the air-pollution deaths each of these tonnes avoids, as a multiple of the world average behind the shared rate, 1.46 air-pollution deaths per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ from fossil fuels (Rethink Priorities). The conversion values every tonne for its heat deaths (discounted over the decades until they come) and adds "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂"'s air-pollution part times this row, at once. Here: the share of ship smoke that goes with each tonne cut times ship smoke per tonne of CO₂. It replaces an earlier, unsourced 40% guess, under which the model had to count either all of the world-average smoke or none.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly by the evaluator (none here)
rows.explainer: A row every climate model has, which the site's conversion reads (docs/normalization.md 2.5): air-pollution deaths the evaluator counts itself, per tonne, on top of what the tonnes carry through air_pollution_weight. The evaluator counts none for this charity, so 0.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for research, technical assistance and policy work: mostly people. Our judgment; we haven't seen this charity's breakdown.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Lawyers, economists and policy staff could typically earn considerably more in law firms, consulting or industry. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar donated
rows.explainer: The tonnes per dollar above; with credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest). The site turns these tonnes into years of healthy life through the deaths they avoid: "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂", its heat part discounted over "Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂" for every tonne, and its air-pollution part, at once, times "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne" above.
